title: Breaking the barriers
hookLine: the manual's test: bandits demand one of four people; metta hands over none

cards: The lifeboat question: one seat left, who gets it? People argue about it at dinner parties and in philosophy classes.
Fifteen hundred years ago, a Buddhist monk in Sri Lanka wrote his own version, as a test for anyone practicing metta. Four people are sitting together. Bandits burst in.
They say: give us one of you. We're going to kill that one. Who do you hand over?
It's a strange question for a book about kindness. But the answer is the point of the last six days.

teach.b: The monk is Buddhaghosa, and the test is in the ninth chapter of the Visuddhimagga. The four people are the ones you've practiced with over these past days: yourself, a dear person, a neutral person, a hostile person.
The bandits demand one. Now watch the manual's answers.
If you think, take the enemy, your metta isn't finished: there's still a barrier around the one you dislike.
Take the stranger: the same. And here's the twist most people don't expect. If you think, take me, spare the others, that's not the answer either.
It sounds noble, but the manual says it still shows a barrier, around yourself. You've made yourself the one who doesn't count.
The test is passed only when you can't find anyone to hand over. Not the enemy, not the stranger, not the friend, not you. Each one's life weighs the same in your heart.

That's what the manual calls breaking the barriers, sima-sambheda: the walls between the categories come down. This is a picture, not a plan for a real emergency, a way of checking where the walls still stand.
Most people, honestly, find a wall somewhere, and the manual doesn't shame anyone for that. It describes the goal: a mind where kindness no longer sorts people into loved, ignored and disliked.
After six days of taking the categories one at a time, this is where they meet. Tomorrow, the circle opens all the way: every direction, every being.

how: Following the Visuddhimagga, Buddhist meditators aim to extend metta equally to themselves, dear, neutral and hostile persons, and teachers use the manual's bandit test to show what that evenness means.

o: a bell rung to start meditation
a vow to protect all who are in danger

games.q: what the answers show — tap the pairs.
p: a wall around the one you dislike
a wall around the neutral one

s: offering yourself to the bandits passes the manual's test
the manual says that still shows a barrier, around yourself.
the test is meant as a plan for real emergencies
it's a picture for checking where the walls in the mind still stand.
the four people are yourself, dear, neutral and hostile
the same four you've practiced with over these past days.

games.q: bandits demand one of four people: you, a friend, a stranger, an enemy. what answer passes the manual's test?
o: find no one to hand over.
games.why: only when no one can be handed over, not even yourself, does the manual say the barriers are broken.

practice: Bring four people to mind sitting in a row, yourself, someone dear, someone neutral, someone difficult, and offer the phrases to all of them at once: may we be safe, may we be happy, may we be healthy, may we live with ease.
If the wish feels stronger for one and thinner for another, that's fine; that's the wall showing itself. Keep the four together, and let the wish move evenly across the row.

wordCard.voice: Sima-sambheda. The breaking of boundaries between people: the manual's test of metta, when bandits demand one of four and you find no one to hand over.

orig.note: Pali: the breaking down of boundaries between persons in metta practice.

carryVoice: Your line: no one handed over. Not the enemy, not the stranger, not you. One hundred and three days in.
